To apply the ratio test we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{{3}^{n}}{n+2}\,{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{n}.$Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{3}^{n+1}{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{n+1}}{n+3}\cdot \frac{n+2}{{3}^{n}{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{3(n+2)}{n+3}(x+\frac{1}{4})| \\  & =|x+\frac{1}{4}|{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{3(n+2)}{n+3} \\  & =|x+\frac{1}{4}|\cdot 3 \\  & =3|x+\frac{1}{4}|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied if $|x+\frac{1}{4}|<\frac{1}{3}.$ Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is $R=\frac{1}{3}.$

questions.problem:
Given that the power series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(x-1)^{n}$ converges at  $x=-3,$ which of the following **must** be true?

I. The series converges at $x=5$

II. The series diverges at $x=-4$

III. The series converges at $x=-2$
questions.worked_solution:
The center of the expansion is $x=1,$ and since the series is convergent for $x=-3,$ this means that the radius of convergence $R$ is *at least* $4,$ i.e., $R\ge 4.$ So, the series is convergent for every point in the interval $[-3,5).$ However, we know nothing about the convergence of the series at any point outside the interval $[-3,5).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14227049/assets/1f6d98b7983946bf60df9bb29bc527af17a63a38834457404c5284b19165e7d5.png)

 

With this in mind, let's check each of our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $5\notin [-3,5),$ we cannot guarantee that the series is convergent at $x=5.$

- Statement II is false. Since $-4\notin [-3,5),$ we cannot guarantee that the series is divergent at $x=-4.$

- Statement III is true. Since $-2\in [-3,5),$ the series is convergent at $x=-2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem:
Find the radius of convergence $R$ for the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x+3)^{n}}{{2}^{{n}^{2}}}=\frac{x+3}{2}+\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{{2}^{4}}+\frac{(x+3)^{3}}{{2}^{9}}+⋯\,.
$$

$R=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To apply the ratio test, we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{(x+3)^{n}}{{2}^{{n}^{2}}}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{\frac{(x+3)^{n+1}}{{2}^{(n+1)^{2}}}}{\frac{(x+3)^{n}}{{2}^{{n}^{2}}}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(x+3)^{n+1}}{{2}^{(n+1)^{2}}}\cdot \frac{{2}^{{n}^{2}}}{(x+3)^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{x+3}{{2}^{(n+1)^{2}-{n}^{2}}}| \\  & =|x+3|{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{2n+1}} \\  & =|x+3|\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for all $-\infty <x<\infty .$  Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is $R=\infty .$

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x-2)^{n}}{n!}=(x-2)+\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{2!}+\frac{(x-2)^{3}}{3!}+⋯\,.
$$

$R=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To apply the ratio test, we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{(x-2)^{n}}{n!}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{\frac{(x-2)^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}}{\frac{(x-2)^{n}}{n!}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(x-2)^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\cdot \frac{n!}{(x-2)^{n}}| \\  & =|x-2|{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1}{n+1} \\  & =|x-2|\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for all $-\infty <x<\infty .$  Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is $R=\infty .$
